concepts.gloss: A deterministic fixed-tape multitape Turing machine that multiplies two n-bit integers exactly in O(n (lg n)^(1-kappa)) time with kappa = 2^(-182), which disproves the n log n optimality conjecture in this model.

concepts.name: Logarithms and exponentials
concepts.gloss: The logarithm log_b x is the exponent to which the base b must be raised to give x, and exp is its inverse, so that log(xy) = log x + log y and b^(log_b x) = x.

concepts.name: Floor and ceiling functions
concepts.gloss: The floor of x is the largest integer not exceeding x, and the ceiling of x is the smallest integer not less than x.

concepts.name: Positional (radix) representation
concepts.gloss: A nonnegative integer written in base b is a finite string of digits, each between 0 and b-1, whose value is the sum of each digit times the corresponding power of b.

concepts.name: Field of two elements
concepts.gloss: The field F_2 has the two elements 0 and 1, with addition given by XOR and multiplication given by AND.

concepts.name: Bitwise XOR
concepts.gloss: XOR of two bits is 1 exactly when the bits differ, and bitwise XOR of two equal-length bit strings applies this to each position.

concepts.name: Modular arithmetic and congruences
concepts.gloss: Two integers are congruent modulo m when they differ by a multiple of m, and addition and multiplication of residue classes modulo m are well defined by working with representatives.

concepts.name: Greatest common divisor and the Euclidean algorithm
concepts.gloss: The gcd of two integers is the largest integer dividing both, two integers are coprime when their gcd is 1, and the Euclidean algorithm computes the gcd by repeated division with remainder.

concepts.name: Prime numbers
concepts.gloss: A prime is an integer greater than 1 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself, and every integer greater than 1 factors uniquely into primes.

concepts.name: Binomial coefficients and counting subsets
concepts.gloss: The binomial coefficient binom(n,k) counts the k-element subsets of an n-element set and equals n!/(k!(n-k)!).

concepts.name: Mathematical induction
aliases: recursion on the number of ranges
concepts.gloss: Induction proves a statement for all natural numbers by proving a base case and showing that the statement for n+1 follows from the statement for n, or from all smaller values in strong induction.

concepts.name: Divide-and-conquer recurrence
concepts.gloss: A divide-and-conquer recurrence expresses the cost on an input of size n in terms of the costs on smaller subproblems plus the cost of combining them, and its solution is found by unrolling the recursion.

concepts.name: Random-access machine model
concepts.gloss: The random-access machine has a finite program and memory cells addressed by integers, so that any cell can be read or written in one step.

concepts.name: Limits and convergence of sequences
aliases: limit as n tends to infinity
concepts.gloss: A sequence converges to L when its terms eventually stay arbitrarily close to L, and the limit of a ratio is the ratio of the limits when both converge.

concepts.name: Convergence of series
concepts.gloss: An infinite series converges when its sequence of partial sums converges, and its sum is the limit of those partial sums.

concepts.name: Geometric series
aliases: sum of powers of a ratio
concepts.gloss: A geometric series is a sum of the form a + ar + ar^2 + ... + ar^k, which equals a(1 - r^(k+1))/(1 - r) for r not equal to 1 and is bounded by a/(1 - r) when |r| < 1.

concepts.name: Big-Omega, big-Theta and little-o notation
concepts.gloss: Omega(f) bounds a function below by a constant multiple of f for large inputs, Theta(f) bounds it both above and below, and o(f) means the ratio to f tends to zero.

concepts.name: Dot product and orthogonal vectors
concepts.gloss: The dot product of two vectors of the same length is the sum of the products of their corresponding entries, and two vectors are orthogonal when this sum is zero.

concepts.name: Matrix product, transpose, and special matrices
concepts.gloss: The product of an m-by-k and a k-by-n matrix is the m-by-n matrix of dot products of rows and columns, the transpose swaps rows and columns, and a diagonal, triangular, or permutation matrix has the stated zero pattern.

concepts.name: Complex modulus, conjugate and polar form
aliases: absolute value of a complex number
concepts.gloss: The modulus |a+bi| of a complex number is sqrt(a^2+b^2), its conjugate is a-bi, and every nonzero complex number can be written as r e^(i theta) with r > 0 and a real angle theta.

concepts.name: Fixed-point arithmetic
concepts.gloss: A fixed-point number is an integer scaled by a fixed power of two, so that arithmetic on such numbers is integer arithmetic with a fixed binary point.

frame.name: frame at vertex r
frame.meaning: The invertible linear operator, the frame, at a source, gate or sink r, acting on arrays indexed by the common address set.
frame.quote: Let $D_r$ denote the frame at a source, gate or sink $r$: an invertible linear operator on the arrays indexed by the common address set, the addresses that every wire's array is indexed by.

frame.name: network vertex
frame.meaning: A source, gate or sink of the network, whose frame is D_r.
frame.quote: Let $D_r$ denote the frame at a source, gate or sink $r$: an invertible linear operator on the arrays indexed by the common address set, the addresses that every wire's array is indexed by.

frame.name: edge target vertex
frame.meaning: The vertex at the other end of an edge that starts at r.
frame.quote: Along an edge from $r$ to $s$, the operator $D_s D_r^{-1}$ turns the stored array $D_r g$ into $D_s g$.

frame.name: logical array
frame.meaning: The array that the computation means, before it is stored in a frame.
frame.quote: The stored array is $D_r g$ when the logical array is $g$, the array the computation means.

frame.name: pointwise linear gate
frame.meaning: A gate of the network that combines its input arrays with fixed scalar coefficients.
frame.quote: A pointwise linear gate $G$ with $t$ inputs, where $t$ is the number of its input arrays, commutes with a common frame: $G(D_r g_1,\ldots,D_r g_t)=D_r\,G(g_1,\ldots,g_t)$.

frame.name: number of gate inputs
frame.meaning: The number of input arrays of the gate G.
frame.quote: A pointwise linear gate $G$ with $t$ inputs, where $t$ is the number of its input arrays, commutes with a common frame: $G(D_r g_1,\ldots,D_r g_t)=D_r\,G(g_1,\ldots,g_t)$.

frame.name: input role
frame.meaning: An input role of the network, whose array is routed by the scalar routing.
frame.quote: The scalar routing sends each input role $w$ to $\rho(w)$, the output role assigned to $w$, and multiplies the array by a sign $\varepsilon_w$, which is $+1$ or $-1$ and is fixed by the network.

frame.name: output role assignment
frame.meaning: The map sending each input role w to the output role assigned to w by the scalar routing.
frame.quote: The scalar routing sends each input role $w$ to $\rho(w)$, the output role assigned to $w$, and multiplies the array by a sign $\varepsilon_w$, which is $+1$ or $-1$ and is fixed by the network.

frame.name: routing sign
frame.meaning: The sign, +1 or -1, that the network fixes and multiplies onto the array of input role w.
frame.quote: The scalar routing sends each input role $w$ to $\rho(w)$, the output role assigned to $w$, and multiplies the array by a sign $\varepsilon_w$, which is $+1$ or $-1$ and is fixed by the network.

frame.name: route start vertex

frame.name: route end vertex
frame.meaning: The vertex where the route from input role w ends, namely the sink of the output role assigned to w.
frame.quote: where $\mathrm{source}(w)$ and $\mathrm{sink}(\rho(w))$ are the vertices where the route starts and ends.

frame.quote: Each frame acts on the wires of a [Linear network that restores auxiliary values](linear-network.md).

linear-network.quote: The network is a linear operator in [Linear algebra over a field](linear-algebra.md).
It has the fixed structure of a [Fixed-tape machine model](fixed-tape-machine.md): its wires and schedule do not depend on the values.

subset-network.quote: It is based on a [Linear network that restores auxiliary values](linear-network.md) of gates that exchange the banks $X_a$ and $Y_a$ with signs.
Each gate and terminal carries a subspace label of one fixed space, so the network is built on [Linear algebra over a field](linear-algebra.md).
The operator on each role is computed from the endpoint frames of the [Frame of a network vertex](frame.md), so only the two ends of a route matter.

fixed-tape-machine: Fixed tracks, meaning several parallel rows of symbols stored in each cell, and finitely many work tapes are harmless for this count.
A scan is one pass of a head across a stretch of tape.
A field is a block of consecutive digits holding one number.

Moving one digit in a fixed radix takes a bounded number of scans, because a digit is one symbol from a fixed alphabet, so the finite control can hold it while the head makes a fixed number of passes.
The control cannot hold a whole field, so each digit must be carried past the other field, and the number of passes grows with the field lengths.
Scans are the unit of cost because a scan takes about as many steps as the cells it crosses, since each step moves a head one cell.
Counting scans therefore counts steps up to a constant factor.
linear-network: md) uses it to swap two banks.
Here $T$ denotes a three-element subset of $[h]$, not the earlier linear map.
Let $\mathcal T$ be the set of all such subsets.
Subsets $S$ and $T$ are neighbors when $|S\cap T|=1$.
Its four gates are:
- copy: add $x_T$ to $A_{ST}$;
- gather: add $\sum_{T\ni i}x_T$ to $C_i$;
- scatter: add $\sum_{i\in S}C_i$ to $y_S$;
- side injection: add $\sum_{T:\,|S\cap T|=1}A_{ST}$ to $y_S$.
Each gate adds a sum of other wires to one wire, so the reversed, negated gate list undoes an invocation.
Rows 0 and 1 subtract exactly the $p$ and $q$ terms that rows 4 and 5 add, so the old scratch contents cancel:
$$y_S\gets y_S+\sum_{i\in S}\sum_{T\ni i}x_T+\sum_{T:\,|S\cap T|=1}x_T.
The first sum gives $x_T$ the coefficient $|S\cap T|$, and the side injection adds $1$ more when $|S\cap T|=1$.
Modulo 2 the total is $1$ only when $|S\cap T|=3$, that is $T=S$, since $1+1=0$.
So $y_S$ becomes $y_S+x_S$ and no other value changes.
This matches the paper's lemma.
Stage 2 is the reversed, negated gate list of a forward invocation from $Y$ to $X$, which adds $Y_a$ to $X_a$; undoing it changes $X_a$ to $X_a-Y_a$.
For single values $X=x$ and $Y=y$ the stages give $(x,y+x)$, then $(-y,y+x)$, then $(-y,x)$.
Every invocation restores its scratch wires, so the composition sends $(X_a,Y_a)\mapsto(-Y_a,X_a)$.
Over $\mathbb F_2$ the sign is immaterial.

background.summary: The reader has an undergraduate computer science education at introductory depth: discrete mathematics (integers, divisibility, modular arithmetic, gcd and primes, binomial coefficients, induction, the field of two elements with XOR), algorithms (the big-O family, divide-and-conquer recurrences, the RAM and multitape Turing models), calculus (limits, convergence of sequences and series, geometric series, basic integrals), elementary linear algebra over the reals and F_2 (vector spaces, linear maps, rank, dot products, matrix products), and complex numbers with modulus and polar form. The reader has not reached specialist algebra, tensor products, bilinear forms, eigen-theory beyond the basics, analysis (liminf and limsup), or numerical analysis, so the main theorem's proof and its network and transform machinery must be explained.
